description: Referee Education, Awareness, and Protection Quiz - Canonical Data

questions.learningObjective: Insults and taunts hurt.
questions.title: A Call You Disagree With
questions.scenario: The ref stops play. You think your team did nothing wrong. What should you do?

options.text: Shout that the ref needs glasses.
Tell the ref they are useless.
Keep asking politely until the ref changes the call.
Accept the call and keep cheering for your team.

questions.reveal: You can disagree and still move on. Asking again and again puts pressure on the ref, even if your voice is calm.

lesson.label: Non-physical abuse · Level 1
lesson.summary: Insults and taunts hurt.
lesson.reference: U.S. Soccer Policy 531-9 · Penalty Summary, p. 6
lesson.detail: Covers belittling an official or undermining their authority.

questions.learningObjective: Do not grab, chase, or corner the ref.
questions.title: After the Game
questions.scenario: Your team loses. You want to talk to the ref, but they are leaving. What should you do?

options.text: Follow the ref until they are alone.
Stand in front of the ref so they cannot leave.
Let them leave. Send your concern to the league later.
Walk after them and calmly explain your side.

questions.reveal: A calm voice does not make following someone okay. Let the ref leave without having to listen to your complaint.

lesson.label: Physical abuse · Level 2
lesson.summary: Do not grab, chase, or corner the ref.
lesson.reference: U.S. Soccer Policy 531-9 · Penalty Summary, p. 12
lesson.detail: Covers confrontational contact and property damage. Examples include pursuing an official to their car.

questions.learningObjective: Online abuse counts too.
questions.title: A Clip Online
questions.scenario: Someone posts a video of a call you think was wrong. You want the league to look at it. What should you do?

options.text: Post insults on the ref’s own page.
Send the clip to the league through its feedback form.
Ask everyone to send angry messages to the ref.
Post the ref’s name so others can politely ask for answers.

questions.reveal: The league can review a concern without a crowd targeting the ref. Sharing their name to send people after them can turn into harassment.

lesson.label: Non-physical abuse · Level 3
lesson.summary: Online abuse counts too.
lesson.reference: U.S. Soccer Policy 531-9 · Penalty Summary, p. 8
lesson.detail: Includes cyberbullying and exposing private information to target an official.

questions.learningObjective: Do not pressure or scare the ref.
questions.title: Let Them Walk Away
questions.scenario: You ask the ref about a call. They say they need to go. What should you do?

options.text: Step back and let them go.
Block their way until they answer.
Get close to their face and shout.
Walk beside them and keep asking in a quiet voice.

questions.reveal: Respecting an answer includes knowing when to stop. Following along keeps the pressure on after the ref has ended the talk.

lesson.label: Non-physical abuse · Level 2
lesson.summary: Do not pressure or scare the ref.
lesson.reference: U.S. Soccer Policy 531-9 · Penalty Summary, p. 7
lesson.detail: Covers harassment and intimidation through words or behavior.

questions.learningObjective: Threatening harm is abuse.
questions.title: A Red Card
questions.scenario: Your teammate gets sent off. You think the ref got it wrong. What should you do?

options.text: Tell the ref they will regret this.
Threaten to hurt the ref after the game.
Ask your teammate to stay while you politely argue the call.
Help your teammate leave the field calmly.

questions.reveal: Help your teammate follow the decision. Keeping them on the field to argue makes things worse, even if you speak politely.

lesson.label: Non-physical abuse · Level 3
lesson.summary: Threatening harm is abuse.
lesson.reference: U.S. Soccer Policy 531-9 · Penalty Summary, p. 8
lesson.detail: Includes threats of violence against officials.

questions.learningObjective: Keep your hands to yourself.
questions.title: Getting Their Attention
questions.scenario: The ref has not heard you. You want to ask a question. What should you do?

options.text: Pull hard on their shirt.
Poke them in the chest.
Wait for a suitable moment and speak without touching them.
Give their shoulder a small tap to get their attention.

questions.reveal: A small tap may sound harmless, but the ref has not agreed to be touched. Use your voice and give them space.

lesson.label: Physical abuse · Level 1
lesson.summary: Keep your hands to yourself.
lesson.reference: U.S. Soccer Policy 531-9 · Penalty Summary, p. 11
lesson.detail: Includes deliberate unwanted touches, even small ones.

questions.learningObjective: Do not grab, chase, or corner the ref.
questions.title: The Ref Is Leaving
questions.scenario: The ref turns away before you finish speaking. What should you do?

options.text: Grab their arm and hold them there.
Let them go and raise your concern with the league later.
Pull them back by their shirt.
Hold their arm gently for just one more sentence.

questions.reveal: Even a gentle hold stops someone from leaving freely. Keeping your hands to yourself matters more than finishing your point.

lesson.label: Physical abuse · Level 2
lesson.summary: Do not grab, chase, or corner the ref.
lesson.reference: U.S. Soccer Policy 531-9 · Penalty Summary, p. 12
lesson.detail: Covers confrontational contact and property damage. Examples include pursuing an official to their car.

questions.learningObjective: Violence has no place in the game.
questions.title: An Angry Fan
questions.scenario: A fan throws a bottle to hit the ref, but misses. What is the safest next step?

options.text: Stay back and get help from event staff right away.
Throw a bottle back at the fan.
Cheer because the bottle missed.
Wait to report it unless the fan tries again.

questions.reveal: Missing does not make the throw safe. Get help now; do not wait for someone to get hurt.

lesson.label: Physical abuse · Level 3
lesson.summary: Violence has no place in the game.
lesson.reference: U.S. Soccer Policy 531-9 · Penalty Summary, p. 13
lesson.detail: Covers violent acts such as striking, spitting, and aiming objects at an official.

questions.learningObjective: Do not pressure or scare the ref.
questions.title: Shouting From the Sideline
questions.scenario: You are angry about several calls and feel like swearing at the ref. What should you do?

options.text: Swear at the ref after every call.
Get other fans to shout insults with you.
Shout your complaint just once so you can get it out.
Take a break from watching until you feel calm.

questions.reveal: Taking a break stops your anger from becoming someone else’s problem. One outburst can still hurt or frighten the ref.

lesson.label: Non-physical abuse · Level 2
lesson.summary: Do not pressure or scare the ref.

questions.learningObjective: Support the person behind the whistle.
questions.title: A Young Ref
questions.scenario: A teenage ref makes a mistake. You are watching from the sideline. What should you do?

options.text: Tell the ref they are too young for the job.
Laugh at them with the other fans.
Keep cheering for the players and let the game continue.
Call out tips after every play to teach them the job.

questions.reveal: Unasked-for tips from the sideline can become constant pressure. Young refs need room to learn, just like players.

lesson.label: Respecting referees
lesson.summary: Support the person behind the whistle.
lesson.reference: U.S. Soccer Policy 531-9 · Penalty Summary, p. 2
lesson.detail: The policy guide encourages everyone to protect officials and keep soccer welcoming.

questions.learningObjective: Insults and taunts hurt.
questions.title: Was That Handball?
questions.scenario: You think the ball hit a player’s hand. The ref lets play go on. What should you do?

options.text: Shout that the ref is cheating.
Let play continue and look up the rule later.
Run onto the field to stop the game.
Hold up your phone and insist the ref watch your replay.

questions.reveal: You may have missed something, and not every touch on a hand is a foul. Your phone is not a reason to stop the game.

questions.learningObjective: Support the person behind the whistle.
questions.title: Time to Cool Down
questions.scenario: A call makes you so angry that you want to yell. What should you do first?

options.text: Step away and take a few slow breaths.
Kick the fence beside the ref.
Shout whatever comes to mind.
Stay by the field and count every mistake the ref makes.

questions.reveal: A real break helps you calm down. Keeping a list of mistakes keeps your attention on the anger.

lesson.reference: U.S. Soccer Policy 531-9 · Penalty Summary, p. 2

questions.learningObjective: Support the person behind the whistle.
questions.title: The Coach Sets the Tone
questions.scenario: You are coaching. Your players look at you after a call they dislike. What should you do?

options.text: Tell them the ref wants them to lose.
Lead the team in mocking the ref.
Tell them to keep asking the ref until the call changes.
Tell them to focus on the next play.

questions.reveal: Players learn from your reaction. Help them get back to playing instead of teaching them to wear the ref down.

questions.learningObjective: Do not attack who someone is.
questions.title: A Hurtful Joke
questions.scenario: A fan makes fun of the ref’s accent. If it feels safe to speak up, what should you say?

options.text: “Say it louder so the ref hears!”
“I have an even better joke about them.”
“That is not okay. Let’s focus on the game.”
“Save that joke for our group chat.”

questions.reveal: Moving a hurtful joke to a private chat does not make it respectful. Someone’s background is never a reason to mock them.

lesson.label: Non-physical abuse · Level 4
lesson.summary: Do not attack who someone is.
lesson.reference: U.S. Soccer Policy 531-9 · Penalty Summary, p. 9
lesson.detail: Covers discriminatory words and actions about identity or background.

questions.learningObjective: Do not grab, chase, or corner the ref.
questions.title: The Ref’s Bag
questions.scenario: You are angry with the ref and standing near their bag. What should you do?

options.text: Kick the bag across the ground.
Leave their things alone and walk away.
Dump everything out of the bag.
Move the bag so the ref has to come and talk to you.

questions.reveal: Using someone’s belongings to force a talk crosses a boundary. Leave their things where they are.

questions.learningObjective: Get help. Report what happened.
questions.title: Someone Is Yelling
questions.scenario: A parent keeps yelling insults at the ref. You are nearby. What is the safest way to help?

options.text: Ask event staff to step in.
Shout insults back at the parent.
Join in so the ref gets the message.
Stand face-to-face with the parent and refuse to move until they stop.

questions.reveal: Get help without starting another fight. Trying to force the parent to stop yourself can put you and others at risk.

lesson.label: Protecting referees
lesson.summary: Get help. Report what happened.
lesson.reference: U.S. Soccer Policy 531-9 · Penalty Summary, p. 15
lesson.detail: Reporting guidance asks for match details, a description, and available unedited evidence through existing reporting channels.

questions.learningObjective: Threatening harm is abuse.
questions.title: You Hear a Threat
questions.scenario: Someone tells the ref, “I will hurt you after the game.” What should you do?

options.text: Laugh and tell them to go ahead.
Threaten to hurt that person back.
Wait until tomorrow to report it, when everyone is calm.
Tell event staff right away. Call emergency services if danger is immediate.

questions.reveal: A threat needs prompt help. Waiting may leave the ref at risk when the game ends.

questions.learningObjective: Do not grab, chase, or corner the ref.
questions.title: Walking Out
questions.scenario: The game is over. You are upset, and the ref is walking out nearby. What should you do?

options.text: Follow them and shout about the score.
Get your friends to surround them.
Give them space and leave with your team.
Wait for them outside so you can have a quiet chat about the call.

questions.reveal: A quiet chat can still feel like being cornered when someone is trying to leave. Use the league’s feedback route later.

questions.learningObjective: Online abuse counts too.
questions.title: A Cruel Post
questions.scenario: You see a post telling people to harass a ref. How can you help?

options.text: Add an insult of your own.
Save evidence and report the post to the platform and league.
Send the post to people who dislike the ref.
Share the post publicly to show everyone how wrong it is.

questions.reveal: Sharing can send more people toward the ref, even when you mean to help. Report it without spreading it.

questions.learningObjective: Get help. Report what happened.
questions.title: Sending Feedback
questions.scenario: You want to raise a concern about how a game was refereed. What should you do?

options.text: Use the league’s feedback channel and describe what happened calmly.
Post that the ref should never work again.
Send the ref an insulting message.
Find the ref’s personal number and call politely.

questions.reveal: A polite tone does not make a personal phone number the right route. The league can handle feedback without invading the ref’s privacy.

questions.learningObjective: Support the person behind the whistle.
questions.title: Making Things Right
questions.scenario: You shouted an insult at the ref. You have calmed down. What should you do?

options.text: Blame the ref for making you angry.
Pretend it never happened and do it again next week.
Follow the ref so you can apologize before they leave.
Stop the behavior and ask the league how to pass on an apology.

questions.reveal: An apology should not force another encounter. Give the ref space, take responsibility, and change what you do next time.

questions.learningObjective: Get help. Report what happened.
questions.title: A Threat in a Message
questions.scenario: Someone sends you a message saying they plan to hurt a ref. What should you do?

options.text: Delete it so nobody gets in trouble.
Reply with ideas for how to scare the ref.
Save the message and report it promptly; get emergency help if danger is immediate.
Post a screenshot for everyone to see who sent it.

questions.reveal: Keep evidence and send it to people who can act. A public post can spread the threat and expose the ref to more harm.

questions.learningObjective: Support the person behind the whistle.
questions.title: A Ref Looks Upset
questions.scenario: Fans have been harsh to a young ref. There is a safe moment to speak, and the ref is happy to talk. What could you say?

options.text: “If you cannot take it, quit.”
“Thanks for being here today. You deserve respect.”
“The fans were right to yell at you.”
“Thanks for coming. Now let me explain all your mistakes.”

questions.reveal: Support does not need a review of every call. A simple thank-you lets the ref feel valued without another lecture.

questions.learningObjective: Do not pressure or scare the ref.
questions.title: A Yellow Card
questions.scenario: You get a yellow card and think it is unfair. The ref tells you to get on with the game. What should you do?

options.text: Accept the card and keep playing.
Clap in the ref’s face to mock them.
Scream that the ref knows nothing.
Calmly keep explaining until the ref agrees to review it.

questions.reveal: A calm voice is good, but continuing after being told to move on is still arguing. Accepting a call does not mean you agree with it.

questions.learningObjective: Do not pressure or scare the ref.
questions.title: In the Way
questions.scenario: You are standing at the gate. The ref needs to walk through. What should you do?

options.text: Shut the gate so they cannot leave.
Tell them they have to push past you.
Ask them to answer one quick question before you move.
Move aside and let them pass.

questions.reveal: Letting someone leave should not come with a condition. Move first and respect their space.

questions.learningObjective: Insults and taunts hurt.
questions.title: Uneven Calls
questions.scenario: You think the ref keeps giving the other team better calls. You want to raise this later. What should you do?

options.text: Shout that the other team paid the ref.
Tell everyone the ref is a cheat.
Send the league clear examples without guessing the ref’s motives.
Send a polite complaint saying the ref must secretly support the other team.

questions.reveal: Describe what you saw, not a motive you cannot know. A polite accusation is still an accusation.

questions.title: A Dangerous Moment
questions.scenario: A teammate says they want to spit at the ref. What should you do?

options.text: Tell them to aim at the ref’s face.
Urge them to step away and get help from the coach.
Join in to show support.
Suggest spitting toward the ref but missing on purpose.

questions.reveal: Aiming to miss does not make spitting toward someone okay. Help stop the situation before anyone acts.

questions.learningObjective: Support the person behind the whistle.
questions.title: Keeping Refs in the Game
questions.scenario: A friend says referees should just put up with insults. What is the best reply?

options.text: “Everyone deserves respect, even when they make mistakes.”
“Yes, paying them means we can say anything.”
“Yes, insults will teach them to do better.”
“We should only shout at the older refs; they can handle it.”

questions.reveal: Respect is for every ref, not just young ones. Age does not make abuse harmless.
